structured_output.summary:
I searched the external sources that bear on the open hypotheses, plus some directions the tree hasn't considered. Six findings are worth acting on:

(1) airbench94_muon rescales every conv filter to a fixed norm before each step and uses only 3 Newton-Schulz iterations. If the port does the same, filter weight decay has no effect. That would make H1.5.4 near-certain and explain why E016 and E022 behaved like changes to the SGD-group weight decay alone. It also means H1.2.3's "5→3 iterations" lever may already be spent.

(2) A 2024 study of weight EMA (arXiv 2411.18704) finds that BatchNorm statistics limit how long an averaging window can be. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, recomputing BN statistics for the EMA model added about 0.55 pp. airbench's Lookahead averages the BN running statistics together with the weights and writes the average back into the model. The final model therefore carries averaged BN statistics, not statistics computed for the averaged weights. This supports testing H1.3.6 and H2.3.3.

(3) Muon's orthogonalization is a small, already-measured cost (E006: +3.8%). Published cheaper variants (Turbo-Muon, cubic Newton-Schulz, Polar Express) claim about 3% end-to-end savings at most, so H1.2.3 is capped at roughly 1–2%.

(4) The FLOP rate implied by airbench's own records (0.29 PFLOP in 2.59 s, 3.1 PFLOP in 27.3 s) is about 112–114 TFLOP/s. This calibrates H2.2.4.

(5) Untested directions:
- FreezeOut (freezing early layers late in training), reported at 20% faster with no accuracy loss for wide ResNets on CIFAR-100.
- Hiverge's brightness/contrast jitter, which it reports improves accuracy at the same step count.
- Hiverge's lighter label smoothing (0.09) and its schedule that shrinks the filter-norm target over training.
- Selective backprop delayed to late training, where Composer's defaults reported about 10% faster at equal accuracy.

(6) There is no public CIFAR-100 recipe beyond the 8.11 s / 75.29% one already in the tree. The organizers' benchmark repo has no pull requests, and that recipe's pull request now returns 404.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon renormalizes every conv filter before each Muon step: `p.data.mul_(len(p.data)**0.5 / p.data.norm())`. It uses 3 Newton-Schulz steps with coefficients (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315), Muon lr 0.24, momentum 0.6 with Nesterov, and batch 2000. The SGD groups use bias_lr 0.053, head_lr 0.67, momentum 0.85 and wd 2e-6*batch_size. Label smoothing is 0.2, the whitening bias trains for 3 epochs and then freezes, BN momentum is 0.6, and LR decays linearly to 0. The script has no Lookahead or EMA.
findings.relevance: If the port copied this renormalization, weight decay on the conv filters does nothing, and only the weight decay on BN biases, the whitening bias and the head acts. That would explain E016 (global wd ×0.5 helped) together with E022 (SGD-group wd ×0.25 did not). It also suggests the port may already run 3 Newton-Schulz steps, not 5, which leaves little for H1.2.3's iteration cut.

findings.claim: Hiverge's evolved CIFAR-10 recipe runs Muon at lr 0.205 and momentum 0.655 with 3 unrolled Newton-Schulz iterations (a=3.4576, b=-4.7391, c=2.0843). It renormalizes filters adaptively (every 2+int(15*progress) steps), and the filter-norm target shrinks over training from 0.5012 to 0.0786. Other settings: wd 1.0418e-6*batch_size, bias lr 0.0573, head lr 0.5415, SGD momentum 0.825, batch 1536, 7.65 epochs, label smoothing 0.09, BN momentum 0.5566 with eps 1e-12, whitening-bias training for 0.2 epoch, and brightness 0.14 / contrast 0.13 color jitter. Its README says the jitter gave higher validation accuracy at the same step count; it does not say by how much.
findings.relevance: The shrinking norm target acts as a weight-decay or effective-LR schedule on the filters. It is an untested lever for the short CIFAR-100 runs (H1.5). The lighter label smoothing (0.09) is far below the port's 0.3; E013 only tested the range 0.2–0.3. Color jitter is an untested augmentation that is cheap on the GPU. Renormalizing only every k steps is the means named in H1.2.3.

findings.claim: LookaheadState is built from `net.state_dict()`. Every 5 steps it lerps all half/float entries, including the BN running_mean and running_var, toward the live net with decay `0.95**5 * (step/total)**3`. It then copies the EMA back into the net with `net_param.copy_(ema_param)`, which resets the fast weights. The final call `update(model, decay=1.0)`. BN layers use eps 1e-12 and frozen weights (scale), with only the bias trained. The whitening bias trains for 3 epochs and then freezes. The script also uses Cutout 12 and translation with reflect padding.
findings.relevance: The final model's BN statistics are an average of running statistics from the fast weights, not statistics recomputed for the averaged weights. That is exactly the case where BN recalibration is known to help (next finding), which supports testing H1.3.6 and H2.3.3. Because the fast weights are reset to the EMA every 5 steps, this is Lookahead, not a plain EMA. H1.3.5 compares those two.

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.18704 (Exponential Moving Average of Weights in Deep Learning: Dynamics and Benefits)
findings.claim: BatchNorm, not the parameters, limits how long the EMA averaging window can be: 'EMAs with the largest averaging windows fail unless BN stats are recomputed'. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, the EMA model scored 77.99% without BN recompute and 78.54% with it (+0.55 pp, Table 10). The authors recompute with a full pass over the training set. EMA works best when averaging at reasonably high LR and is strong early in training.
findings.relevance: This directly supports trying BN recalibration after the final Lookahead/EMA swap. On a 32 px forward pass of about 5k images the cost is far below 0.15 s. The gain could be larger here than in the paper, because the EMA statistics also average over the 24/28 px phases.

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04632 (Turbo-Muon); https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00371 (How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need?); https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16932 (Polar Express)
findings.claim: Turbo-Muon's preconditioning removes one of 5 Newton-Schulz iterations and claims about 3% end-to-end time savings on fast-training benchmarks. The 2606.00371 study finds training quality is not tied to orthogonalization accuracy: a cubic 5-step schedule (10 matmuls instead of 15) gets within about 1e-3 validation loss of quintic Muon, and several orthogonalizers, including exact SVD, give indistinguishable GPT-2 Small loss. Polar Express converges about 2× faster than Newton-Schulz to a given error.
findings.relevance: This caps the payoff of H1.2.3. Muon overhead measured in E006 was +3.8%, and it is presumably smaller in E016, where groups run at lower resolution part of the time but the filter count is unchanged. Even halving the Newton-Schulz cost saves at most about 1–2% of total time. Accuracy is unlikely to suffer, given how robust Muon is to approximate orthogonalization.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon: 94.01% in 2.59 s at 0.29 PFLOP. airbench96_faster: 96.00% in 27.3 s at 3.1 PFLOP. The implied rate is about 112–114 TFLOP/s on an A100. airbench94 with SGD took 3.83 s and about 9.9 epochs. The Muon version runs 8 epochs, also at batch 2000, with widths 64/256/256 and TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: This gives the reference throughput for H2.2.4: the port should reach at least about 90 TFLOP/s at 32 px. On CIFAR-10, Muon cut epochs about 19% (9.9→8) and time about 32% (3.83→2.59 s). The batch size also changed, so like E006 this does not separate Muon from the batch change, which is the question H1.2.2 asks.

findings.claim: In the CIFAR-10 ablation path, the epochs needed for 94% fall as each component is added: whitening 45→21, Dirac 21→18, bias scaling 18→13.5, Lookahead 13.5→12.0, multi-crop TTA 12.0→10.8, alternating flip 10.8→9.9. At 20 epochs without Cutout, alternating flip beats random flip 93.87% to 93.74%, which the paper rates as worth 27% of training time. On CIFAR-100 with CIFAR-10 hyperparameters left untuned, airbench96 reaches 79.27% (79.76% with Cutout), about 1.7 pp above ResNet-18.
findings.relevance: With TTA banned, the about-10% epoch saving from multi-crop is unavailable, which is the premise of H1.4. Alternating flip is a large lever and should be kept. The CIFAR-100 result again shows the hyperparameters were not tuned for CIFAR-100 (H1.5).

findings.claim: FreezeOut freezes early layers progressively during training: each layer's LR is annealed to zero by its own cutoff (t0 about 0.5), and the layer is then dropped from the backward pass. On CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 it gave about 20% wall-clock savings with no accuracy loss for wide ResNets, 20% savings with 3% loss for DenseNets, and nothing for VGG.
findings.relevance: This is a new direction for H2 that the tree hasn't considered. Group 1 and the whitening layer run at the highest resolution, so their weight-gradient and input-gradient backward cost is a large share of FLOPs. Freezing group 1 (or stopping backprop into it) for the last 20–30% of steps could save several percent. The 32 px tail is where most of the time goes (0.89 s/epoch). Unlike H2.5.2, it keeps the layer's representational capacity.

findings.claim: Selective-Backprop claims up to 3.5× faster convergence to a target error on CIFAR-10/100 in long runs. Composer's tuned defaults apply it only between 50% and 90% of training, keep 50% of each batch, run every other batch, and select on inputs downscaled ×0.5. With those defaults, ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10 trained 8% faster (35m33s→32m36s) at +0.16 pp accuracy. Composer warns that cutting more data for longer hurts accuracy.
findings.relevance: In a 9-epoch run the documented gains are about 10% at best, and they depend on full-data training early and late. Selecting on a cheap low-resolution forward pass and skipping only the backward pass of easy examples is a cheaper variant than airbench96_faster's separate proxy model. The low prior on H2.4 is reasonable, but the 'mid-training only, 0.5× resolution selector' variant is the version worth testing.

findings.claim: The only public CIFAR-100 speedrun result found is the airbench-adapted recipe at 75.29% in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4. Its author noted that official PCIe 300 W times will probably be slower. The organizers' benchmark repo shows 0 pull requests. The baseline is ResNet9 at width 64 for 40 epochs: 75.36% in 59.30 s, measured on 2 Oct 2026.
findings.relevance: The current tip (about 6.55 s) is already well ahead of any public CIFAR-100 recipe, so further gains must come from first principles. The SXM-vs-PCIe caveat supports budgeting accuracy headroom for transfer to the judge's GPU (H4.3).

findings.claim: In the CIFAR-10 speedrun, Fable's progressive resizing (24→28→32) cut time 7.6% (1.98 s→1.828 s), on top of pooling, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion changes. The competing agents' gains came mostly from tuning schedule length (10.5→9.0–9.75 epochs). The disqualified tricks were precomputing augmentation outside the timed region (about 150 ms), picking faster machines, and untimed GPU cooldowns.
findings.relevance: These results agree with the tree's findings: resizing is the main per-epoch FLOP lever (E007), and the epoch dial does most of the work. The disqualified tricks mark the rule boundary; for example, augmentation must stay inside timed train().

findings.claim: Among budget-aware LR schedules, plain linear decay to zero is robust and usually performs best under fixed small budgets.
findings.relevance: This agrees with E009: with Lookahead on, the shape of the schedule's tail barely matters. Further gains from reshaping the LR schedule are unlikely, so tuning effort is better spent on weight decay, the filter-norm target and BN calibration.
